notes.claim: Third and other triple harmonic currents of a three-phase load are additive in the neutral and give additional heating of the cables, while the fundamentals of a balanced load cancel there.
Loads such as rectifiers, variable-speed drives and fluorescent lighting banks draw non-sinusoidal currents, so current can appear in the neutral where a balanced motor load would have none.

The neutral current can reach about 173% of phase current in a balanced system with these pulses, and one paper puts triplen neutral current at up to 3 times the phase fundamental, depending on how the percentage is referred.
The slides take the neutral current as Ibn = 3 × h × IL (3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.5 A at 35%), which exceeds the 150 A line current, so Ibn becomes Ib.
The Table 4Aa bands in the slides: line current governs with factor 0.86 for 15 to 33% third harmonic, and above 33% the factor is applied to a calculated neutral current, not the line current.
Harmonics are only considered when the manufacturer's data says one is present; with no neutral conductor there can be no current in it.
The slides' worked example uses It ≥ 160 / (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) with the harmonic rating factor included in the divisor.

Table 4Aa, as the slides give it, has four bands by the third harmonic of the line current: 0 to 15% line current with factor 1.0, 15 to 33% line current with 0.86, 33 to 45% neutral current with 0.86, and over 45% neutral current with 1.0; the same table appears in IEC 60364-5-52 (E.52.1) as set out in the Schneider guide, and an IET forum answer ties it to Appendix 4 of BS 7671:2018+A2:2022.

The neutral current is 3 × h × IL: the third and other triple harmonics of the three lines add in the neutral to a magnitude equal to the sum of the third harmonic content of each phase, which is why the slides call the neutral higher than the line at 35% (row 3) and take Ibn as Ib.

Above 33% the neutral current is the larger, so the cable is sized on it; at 45% it is 135% of the line current and the three line conductors are then not fully loaded, which is why the factor goes back to 1.0 above 45%; the Schneider guide works 40% (37 × 0.4 × 3 = 44.4 A, ÷ 0.86 = 51.6 A) as an example.

The ordinary current tables assume three loaded conductors; a harmonic neutral makes a fourth, and BS 7671 treats a neutral as a loaded conductor where a third harmonic or its multiples present a distortion above 15% of the line current (523.6.1) or where it carries current without a matching fall in the line conductors (523.6.3). NICEIC words the 15% as total harmonic distortion where the slides say the third harmonic.
notes.contested: The slides and Table 4Aa speak of the third harmonic content of the line current; NICEIC's summary of Regulation 523.6.1 speaks of total harmonic distortion greater than 15% of the fundamental. Makers usually print a THD figure, so the figure the lesson uses is a practice value for the third harmonic, said so.

notes.claim: Where the neutral current comes only from an imbalance in the line currents, the neutral's heat is offset by less heat in a line conductor, so the cable is sized on the highest line current (NICEIC on 523.6.2); harmonic current is the case where there is no such offset.

The slides' worked example runs from the neutral current to the cable: Ibn 157.5 A is Ib, In 160 A from Fig 3A3(b), It = 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86), and Table 4D1A column 5 gives 240 mm² at 346 A (his copy of the table, p.448, row 240: Reference Method B, three or four loaded cables, 346 A).

Harmonics are considered only when the maker's data says there are some, and then the maker's percentage goes into the same sums; makers print THD, not the third harmonic alone: a Thorn luminaire datasheet gives THD 15.00 %, and a Philips Advance (US, 60 Hz) ballast table gives fluorescent ballasts as less than 25% THD (conventional magnetic), less than 20% (standard electronic) and less than 10% (Centium electronic).

No limit is quoted here for a fluorescent fitting's third harmonic in the showroom's drawing: the ANSI standard for electronic ballasts allows a maximum THD of 32%; IEC 61000-3-2 Class C (lighting, input current up to 16 A per phase) limits the third harmonic to 30 × the circuit power factor in percent; the absolute harmonic current matters more than the percentage; and the On-Site Guide says discharge-lighting final circuits must carry the lamps' and controlgear's harmonic currents (its ×1.8 volt-ampere rule includes harmonic current).
